item.title: Let’s talk about Artificial Intelligence (I)
item.description:
# Let’s talk about Artificial Intelligence (I) ## After quite a few conversations on the subject, my impression is that within the evangelical world, Artificial Intelligence is being used far more widely than is openly acknowledged, and that almost no one explains how they do it. **A large part of my working day is now spent in conversation with a machine.**
I’ve been working like this for several years now, using the major conversational AI assistants – Gemini, ChatGPT and Claude – which have gradually become part of almost everything I do, from writing to audio transcription, translation, image generation, video editing, or that much less glamorous but equally necessary task of opening an Excel spreadsheet crammed with nested formulas, cross-references and columns that nobody can remember who created or for what purpose, and managing to extract something from it that a human being can understand. At this stage, practically my entire workflow runs through a system built on a combination of AIs.
Over this time, I’ve seen them change from one quarter to the next, both in terms of what they can do and the way in which one ends up working with them.
There are pastors who use AI to organise the outline of a sermon, to expand on an idea that fell short on Thursday evening, or to put together the Sunday service``
My situation may be more intense than that of most people, as I consider myself a regular—even advanced—user of these tools. But this is no isolated anomaly: artificial intelligence is already part of the day-to-day work of many churches, even though we hardly ever talk about it.
There are pastors who use artificial intelligence to prepare the PowerPoint presentations that are then shown on Sundays; there are those who use it to organise the outline of a sermon, to find an illustration that’s missing, to expand on an idea that fell short on Thursday evening, or to put together the Sunday service, and I won’t even get into the posters for campaigns, concerts and days of prayer – an area where quite a few pastors have finally found an outlet for all the visual creativity they’ve been harbouring, with results that graphic designers across half the world are still gazing at, having not quite recovered from the shock.
In the academic world, where this ceased to be a novelty quite some time ago, the phenomenon has reached proportions that it would be absurd to deny. According to Eurostat data for 2025, [59 per cent of young Spaniards use generative artificial intelligence](https://theobjective.com/sociedad/2026-01-05/jovenes-espanoles-ia-estudiar/) for educational purposes, compared with [a European average of 39 per cent](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/w/edn-20260210-1), which places us at the forefront of Europe by a fairly wide margin; and the CYD Foundation’s report [Use and Perception of AI in the University Environment](https://www.fundacioncyd.org/publicaciones-cyd/uso-y-percepcion-de-la-ia-en-el-entorno-universitario/), published in July 2026 based on a sample of 800 students, raises the figure to 90 per cent among university students, with the added detail that one in four admits to attending fewer classes as a result.
When a tool appears that promises the same result with half the effort, we don’t usually need much persuading``
That Spain tops this European table – and I say this with all due affection for our own country – has not surprised me in the slightest, because we are a nation with a rather long-standing affinity for taking shortcuts, and when a tool appears that promises the same result with half the effort, we don’t usually need much persuading here. What I haven’t been able to find anywhere – and I confess I’ve looked for it – is the equivalent percentage amongst students at our faculties of theology, a figure I’d love to know, though I suspect it would keep more than a few people awake at night.
# What isn’t being said After quite a few conversations on the subject, my impression is that within the Spanish evangelical world, artificial intelligence is being used far more widely than is openly acknowledged, and that almost no one explains how they do it, so that we have neither a manual, nor a shared set of guidelines, nor hardly any accounts from anyone willing to say quite naturally, ‘I prepared this in this way, using this tool, giving it these instructions, and then I checked it in this other way’.
The first is a sort of vague sense of shame, whereby admitting that one has used artificial intelligence is tantamount to confessing that one did not actually do it oneself, that it was handed to one ready-made, and that the credit, if any, belongs to someone else; and as nobody wants to be seen in that light, especially in front of an audience that regards them with respect, they keep quiet and carry on.
The result, in either case, is the same, namely that the Church is indeed using artificial intelligence whilst carefully refraining from discussing it, maintaining an outdated discourse on a new practice and claiming we do things one way when we are actually doing them another.
# Those who do not wish to, and those of us who cannot sit still ###### Do you see a need for this kind of journalism? - Let’s talk about Artificial Intelligence (I)

item.title: The Trailblazing School on the Frontier of Artificial Intelligence
item.description:
# The Trailblazing School on the Frontier of Artificial Intelligence On a Friday morning in early March, about 100 students at Washington Leadership Academy (WLA), a public charter secondary high school in the District of Columbia, gathered in the assembly hall for a “Hackathon,” a hands-on event designed to teach students how generative artificial intelligence (AI) can be used in real life. The Hackathon gave the students a challenge: build a chatbot powered by AI to address real-world needs and problems.
One junior offered a more precise critique than many adults: “The term ‘artificial intelligence’ isn’t real because to be intelligent you have to be able to teach yourself.
A senior showed me a personal AI receptionist he had built on his own time that answers emails, handles phone calls, and organizes calendars, which he hopes to sell to local businesses.
Most of the school’s teachers are using AI. In a [February 2025](https://dccharters.org/blog/guest-blog-at-wla-ai-is-happening-now) survey, 85 percent reported using it professionally, with more than 80 percent doing so on a daily or weekly basis.
They input their country into a chatbot to see whether they could survive a three-year simulated war against Clarksonia, allocating its population across soldiers, scientists, artists, and educators, and selecting a key natural resource.
Niyesha Coleman, the school’s math instructional coach, built a gamified chatbot that walked students through practice problems, offering hints and feedback in a voice trained to sound like hers.
Teachers at WLA, meanwhile, are using AI to support students in ways that weren’t previously possible.
So, he created an AI tool that generated questions modeled on the few already released by the College Board.
WLA teachers are also using AI to address the day-to-day administrative challenges that plague their professional lives.
Clarkson, for example, uses AI to generate a weekly newsletter for the parents of his 86 students, something he says he would never have time to do otherwise.
AI now centralizes daily attendance data on a single dashboard, synthesized with a historical record of absences so that staff can identify and reach out to struggling students before their truancy becomes chronic.
With tools like ChatGPT, students can generate full assignments in seconds, raising questions about authorship, original thinking, and academic integrity.
Tasks focused on summary, recall, or formulaic response are often the easiest for AI to complete and may require little analysis or creativity from students if they do undertake them on their own.
With the development of AI tools that collect increasingly granular information about how students think, write, and learn, schools have been left to figure out their own guardrails for protecting student data.
